I recently completed AI in Health Care: From Strategies to Implementation, an 8 week executive education program through Harvard Medical School . That's certificate 1 of 3 done, two more to go. Honestly, I went in expecting to learn about everything AI can do in healthcare. What I actually walked away with was a much clearer picture of why so many AI tools never make it from the lab into real patient care. A few things that have stuck with me: An accurate model is not a useful product. A model can hit impressive numbers in testing, but if it doesn't fit how clinicians actually work, if the alert comes at the wrong time or adds one more click to an already overloaded day, it simply doesn't get used. More data does not automatically mean a better model. The quality of the data, how outcomes are defined, and who is represented in it matter far more than how much of it you have. Bias can hide in places no one thinks to look. One study we covered showed AI models could predict a patient's race from chest X-rays when experienced radiologists could not. If a model can pick up on something like that, it can also quietly learn the inequities buried in historical health data and repeat them. That stopped me in my tracks. Deployment is the beginning, not the finish line. Healthcare keeps changing, and an AI tool that performed well on day one can quietly stop performing well a year later if no one is monitoring it. I also developed and pitched my own AI healthcare solution as part of the program, working through the unmet need, the data, the stakeholders, the workflow and the regulatory side. That exercise alone changed how I look at any AI tool put in front of me now. So here's my question for those of you in healthcare or building with AI: what do you think is the bigger barrier to AI actually improving patient care right now, the technology itself or how we implement it? Would love to hear your take. #AIinHealthcare #HarvardMedicalSchool #ArtificialIntelligence #HealthcareInnovation #Healthcare

A new milestone for LEAD Development. Together with Emirates Palace Company and Mandarin Oriental Hotel Group, we unveiled Emirates Palace, Mandarin Oriental Mansions, Abu Dhabi. 35 private uniquely designed residences that caters to homeowners who desire to have an address within the grounds of Emirates Palace, with completion anticipated in 2029. This project is only possible because of Abu Dhabi itself, a capital whose leadership has, over decades, built the conditions for opportunities like this to happen. The vision, the long-term planning, first class infrastructure and safe haven environment that define this city are what allow custodians like EPCO to open a chapter of this significance, and what give partners like Mandarin Oriental and ourselves the confidence to create a residential community that compliments unparalleled guest experience provided by Emirates Palace. The mansions uniquely designed and located along pristine shores where the true meaning of place making is embodied. For the first time, private ownership is being introduced within one of the UAE’s most historically and institutionally significant destinations. Thirty-five families will live where, until now, only the Palace has stood. The reception from media, partners, and friends of all three organizations has been remarkable . On behalf of the Lead Development team, our sincere thanks to the leadership of EPCO, Mandarin Oriental, and those who brought this forward, and to the wise leadership of Abu Dhabi that continues to make ambitions of this scale possible. The real work begins now! #EmiratesPalace #MandarinOriental #LEADDevelopment #AbuDhabi

Supporting healthcare professional education across international markets has been an exciting opportunity to broaden my perspective on medical education and diabetes care globally. I’m grateful for the past 8 years at Novo Nordisk, where I learned from the incredible Chronic Disease Education team and had the opportunity to advance patient-centered education. Those experiences have shaped how I approach leadership, learning, and collaboration, and I’ll carry those lessons forward into this next chapter. I’m excited for the opportunity to work with colleagues around the world to advance medical education and help improve the lives of people living with diabetes. If you’re passionate about medical education, diabetes technology, or HCP learning, I’d love to connect and exchange ideas. #MedicalAffairs #MedicalEducation #DiabetesTechnology
